paragraphs.text: The Apostle James opens his epistle with the words “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus” to show the divinity of the Lord Christ. Although he was called the brother of the Lord, he remained humble and called himself a servant of Jesus Christ. Just as a servant has no authority over his own body, his wife or his children, so the Apostle James says that he is a “servant” with joy, because he has surrendered his whole life and his possessions to the Lord, as the Virgin Mary said, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord.” Her joy that she would be the mother of God the Word incarnate did not make her forget that she was a handmaid of God.

The Dispersion: the Christians of Jewish origin were scattered throughout the world after the martyrdom of Stephen because of persecution, so the Apostle James wrote them this epistle to strengthen and encourage them and to reinforce their faith. He also wrote to all believers who were persecuted and to all the Jews who had believed and who had formerly lived among the Gentiles.
May we not forget that we are servants of God, and may we surrender our whole life to Him, however much boldness of sonship we have.

(2) How do we endure trials? (vv. 2-12:) 2 “My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; 3 Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. 4 But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing. 5 If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him. 6 But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed. 7 For let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord. 8 A double minded man is unstable in all his ways. 9 Let the brother of low degree rejoice in that he is exalted: 10 But the rich, in that he is made low: because as the flower of the grass he shall pass away. 11 For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways. 12 Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life, which the Lord hath promised to them that love him.”
Count it: consider it.
All joy: trials bring many blessings that gladden the soul.

Fall: this means that trials come upon the believer from outside, but without the person falling into sin. This kind of trial is to prove the person, as God tested Abraham. God gives the trial according to what a person can bear, but if the person sins during the trial, as Job murmured, God supports him until he repents, and in this way he also benefits from the trial.

When God allows trials to come upon us, we are not troubled, but we trust in the many blessings we shall receive from them, and our hearts rejoice. The following verses show the blessings of trials, which are:
1- Patience:
The first means of enduring a trial and succeeding in it is to be patient in it, because pain is hard for a person, but by being patient in it we receive blessings.
2- Works of perfection:

The second means is to accompany patience with spiritual works such as prayer, fasting, prostrations (metanoias) and thanksgiving, and to continue in these works, striving toward Christian perfection. Thus we grow spiritually in our relationship with God.
3- Wisdom:

A trial creates problems, so a person is perplexed about how to act and needs wisdom to act well and pass through the trial. The Apostle offers a simple solution, which is to ask for it from God in faith, and He will surely give. His giving is marked by two things:
a- Abundantly and generously, more than we ask.
b- With fatherly love, so He does not upbraid us for our weakness and ignorance, but on the contrary covers us and honors us.
4- Faith:

God is ready to give us wisdom, but on condition of faith, and that we be ready to do what He asks of us and trust that the trial is for our good. As for the one who wavers, that is, the doubter, he is like a wave of the sea, which rises and rushes to the shore and then draws back. Such a person lives anxious and disturbed, unable to make the right decision. For the mind of the one who wavers is not convinced that God’s way is the best, and such a one must be sure that he will not receive anything from the Lord, because he does not believe in God’s wisdom and power.

A double minded man: a person who wavers between relying on God and depending on his own mind, his abilities and the powers of the world; or who wavers between holding to God’s commandments and using the evil means of the world, so that he uses one course at times and then the other. Such a person will suffer disturbance and instability in all the affairs of his life.
5- Humility:

The spiritual person, facing a trial, remembers his sins, repents and prays with lowliness before God, and when he humbles himself in this way, God removes from him the feelings of distress and comforts his heart, so his spirit is lifted up and he blesses God and thanks Him. This is the rejoicing in God’s raising him up, that is, thanksgiving.
6- Being a stranger to the world:

The one who feels that he is a stranger to the world and that it passes away can accept the trial and the loss of material things, because in his sight they are transient. The Apostle likens them to flowers that quickly fall to the ground and wither. Therefore it is fitting for the rich, and likewise for each one of us, to feel that everything we own is transient, so that if trials take it away we are not troubled, and we trust that the true wealth is in life with God and the Kingdom of Heaven. But whoever depends on material things will wither like them, that is, he will not enjoy true happiness with God on earth and will receive nothing in heaven.

The Apostle concludes his words about enduring trial by giving good news to the one who endures it, following the means mentioned before in the previous verses and passing through the trial successfully: he receives the heavenly crown in the Kingdom, that is, enjoyment with God forever.

Do not be troubled by the trials that pass over you. However hard they seem, trust that God’s help will not leave you, and that God allowed them so that you may advance in your spiritual life and be delivered by them from every evil.

entries.section: (3) Inward temptations and the goodness of God

paragraphs.text: When he is tempted: he fell into sin because of the temptation.

He moves on to another kind of temptation, the inward temptations, that is, the heart’s responding to evil and falling into sin. If this happens, a person must not think that God is the One who created in him a nature inclined to evil or pushed him into evil by this temptation. Why? Because God is righteous, holy and perfect, so no one can tempt Him, in the sense of making Him fall into sin. And so, because He is luminous, He does not by nature incline toward darkness or toward making people fall into it, in the sense of tempting them in order to make them fall.
As for the former trials, which are a divine testing, they mean God’s attempt to raise a person to higher degrees in order to reward him with a greater reward.

entries.section: (3) Inward temptations and the goodness of God

paragraphs.text: The true cause of falling into temptation is the stirring of lust in a person’s heart and his being deceived by the devil’s wiles, so that he is drawn to the outward pleasure of sin and falls into its evil and bitterness.

entries.section: (3) Inward temptations and the goodness of God

paragraphs.text: He makes clear the seriousness of inward response and of falling into temptation. A person is drawn to the pleasure of sin by his evil carnal inclinations, and this he likens to conception. Lust makes a person fall into actual sin, and he likens sin to the child born of the conception. Then the penalty of sin is death and eternal torment. So if a person continues in his sins all his life, his sin is completed and he is condemned to eternal death. This is like a person who desires to possess, so he falls into the sin of theft and is then sentenced to prison; this is a temptation to which a person responded inwardly with evil feelings. The opposite is Joseph the righteous, who endured slavery in the house of Potiphar and then the sufferings of prison, and received God’s reward, which was the throne of Egypt. This was an outward trial to prove Joseph and reward him.

Driving out evil thoughts saves you from many sins. Satan breaks up your strength and weakens you with a multitude of thoughts, so that when he presents actual sin to you afterward, your fall is easy. So guard against thoughts, sights and words, lest you fall into hard temptations that destroy your life.

entries.section: (3) Inward temptations and the goodness of God

paragraphs.text: The Apostle forbids us to accuse God of being the cause of our sins and problems. The cause of our sins, as he mentioned, is our being drawn by our lusts toward evil, but God is good and the source of all blessings.

entries.section: (3) Inward temptations and the goodness of God

paragraphs.text: Father of lights: the source of all light and good on earth.

With whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning: the planets revolve and their position changes, and from this results the change of climate in the seasons of the year and the succession of night and day; and in ancient times time was known by the shadow. But God has nothing of this, because He is constant and perfect.

The Apostle declares that the source of all the good gifts we enjoy, and of all the talents and abilities we have, is God, the Giver of blessings, and that He is constant and continuous in His giving, not like changeable human beings, who, however good they seem, change and die.

entries.section: (3) Inward temptations and the goodness of God

paragraphs.text: The word of truth: Christ.

A kind of firstfruits of his creatures: in ancient times the Jews offered the firstfruits of their crops and their animals to God, and these were holy and distinct from the rest because they belonged to God. So believers are the firstfruits of the world, so that many others may believe, and because of them God blesses the whole earth with the animals and plants in it.

The greatest grace we have received is the new birth through Baptism, so we became children of Christ the Savior and the beginning of the Church, which will include the many who will believe throughout the ages.

entries.section: (4) The conduct of the children of God

paragraphs.text: The Apostle draws the believer’s attention to some important virtues in his life, namely that he be:

1- Swift to hear: the person who listens well understands more and finds an opportunity to ask God to guide him in what he will say; he is also restful to others and establishes a stronger relationship of love with them, and the result is that he is slow to speak, that is, not impulsive. As Solomon the Wise says, “Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him” (Prov 29:20). So then, should we be silent or speak? The saints say, “Speaking for God’s sake is good, and silence for God’s sake is good also.”
2- Slow to wrath: the true Christian does not become angry with others, but is like his heavenly Father, who is longsuffering, “for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.”
But the acceptable anger is a person’s anger at himself, that is, repentance, and it is also called holy anger.

3- Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness: when a person calms down in his speech with others, he must attend to repentance and the rejection of every kind of filthiness, whether evil thoughts, bad sights, foul speech, all acts of fornication, and the many evils connected with them.

4- Receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls: repentance gives a person purity, so he receives the word of God that he reads in the Holy Bible or hears in the Church and submits to it with humility and calm, and the word is implanted in his heart, affects him and leads him in the way of salvation. This shows the importance of reading the word of God and attending spiritual meetings.

entries.section: (4) The conduct of the children of God

paragraphs.text: 5- Doers of the word: because whoever hears and does not do deceives himself that he is religious and knows much, but the measure is not knowledge but carrying out the commandment in practice.

entries.section: (4) The conduct of the children of God

paragraphs.text: The Apostle likens the one who hears the word and does not do it to a man who looks in a mirror and does not correct his appearance, but goes away and forgets his defects. The believer, however, must look attentively into the word of God, which is a mirror that reveals to him his weakness, his faults and his shortcomings, and so he receives it with meekness and corrects himself, striving toward holiness, truth and perfection, so as to be like his heavenly Father and to keep the image he received by the new birth.

entries.section: (4) The conduct of the children of God

paragraphs.text: If the Law of Moses was commands in the letter, with ordinances and judgments that a person carried out as a slave, as a duty and an obligation, and then forgot them, the law of Christ is otherwise, for it is the law of the freedom of the children of God, out of love. It is called the perfect law because it brings a person to perfection by grace and the work of the Holy Spirit. And whoever abides in the word of God, applying it in his life, his works are blessed by God and he enjoys joy and peace.

entries.section: (4) The conduct of the children of God

paragraphs.text: 6- Bridling his tongue: whoever believes himself to be holy and religious but does not control his tongue deludes himself with a false piety and deceives himself that he knows God when he does not know Him, because he rages, becomes angry, curses and judges others, and thinks that he has become a reformer of them.

entries.section: (4) The conduct of the children of God

paragraphs.text: 7- Mercy: the Apostle James sums up the concept of pure religion as:
1- Works of compassion joined to faith, and mercy toward orphans and widows who have no one to provide for them.
2- A person’s keeping his heart in purity and holiness and the cleanness of thought, and putting the word of God into practice in his life with patience, love and joy.
Therefore the believer should keep away from every source of pollution of hearing and sight, so that he may be sanctified to God in body, soul and spirit.

Offer your love to all around you and have compassion on everyone, for there is no person who is not exposed to troubles. Care especially for those whom others do not care for, or who suffer from a sense of loneliness, and trust that this work of mercy fills your heart with peace, pours God’s mercies upon you, and gladdens your heart when you see the smile on the faces of those to whom you showed mercy.
Love, faith and works

Baptism gives believers a new birth, so that they all become brothers without distinction, bias or preferring one believer over another, but all are members of the one Body of Christ. True faith is bound to love for all without distinction, because Christ, the Lord of glory, will show partiality to no one in heaven but will glorify all with Him, each one according to his works, without regard to his position or wealth or any worldly abilities he has.
Your assembly: he did not say “your church”, because partiality does not befit the Church, and by it she becomes like a Jewish synagogue.

He rebukes their partiality to the rich man, whom he describes as having splendid clothes and gold rings, so they give him a great place to sit in. But the poor man, whose clothes are shabby and dirty, they do not give the right to sit beside the rich man, but he stands far off or sits on the ground. The seriousness of the sin of partiality appears in two matters:
1- Partiality is far from faith, since it considers that the rich are the pillar of the Church and not God who gave them wealth.

2- Partiality is an insult to the poor person, who is created in the image of God, and it is an insult to Christ Himself, who became poor to enrich us, as they said of Him, “Is not this the carpenter’s son?”
Moreover, by it we belittle brothers of ours in the faith, who are members of the one Body of Christ.
Are ye not then partial in yourselves: partiality is far from the fear of God. So you who show partiality, will you not review yourself and doubt this conduct of yours, so as to repent of it?
Partiality springs from evil thoughts, so he asks them to judge their consciences, that is, to be judges of their evil thoughts, review them and repent of them.

The Apostle shows that material wealth does not matter to God, and that many of the saints were poor, such as Moses the shepherd, whom God called from the bush, and David the shepherd, whom God anointed king, and likewise most of the disciples of Christ were fishermen and poor people. These became heirs of the heavenly Kingdom that He prepared for them. He shows the importance of spiritual wealth through faith on earth and the inheritance of the Kingdom, and this is better than all material wealth.
This does not mean that wealth is evil, but the evil is that a person forgets God because of his preoccupation with wealth and falls into pride.

The believers in the Church were influenced by wealth, so they honored the rich and despised the poor, and forgot that wicked rich people use their money and influence to insult the believers and stir up the wicked against them (Acts 19:25-29), and likewise to bring them to trial and throw them into prisons.
The rich go on in their evil and blaspheme the name of Christ by which the believers are called.

May you look to God who stands before you, so that you declare the truth and show partiality to no one out of fear of his position or authority, or for any benefit you hope for from him, and honor everyone, however weak or poor they may be.
The royal law: that is, the law of Christ, the heavenly King, and it is love.

The law of Christ, that is, His rule, is love, and this moves us to love all around us, in application of the commandment “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Lev 19:18), so the Apostle blesses the conduct of love toward all.
Partiality is against love, for it is a transgression of the rule of Christianity and is counted a great sin.

Do not justify yourselves by keeping many commandments and acts of worship in the Church while transgressing the most important thing, which is love, the spirit of the law of Christ, for by this you are guilty toward Christ and all His commandments.

Persisting in one sin deserves death. It is not right to persist in a sin such as murder while being careful about adultery, for the Law of Moses sentences the murderer to death because he broke this commandment, despite his care for the rest of the law.
The law of liberty: the rule of Christ, that is, love.
So in the New Testament we must hold fast to all His commandments and not persist in neglecting one of them by persisting in partiality, for this deserves destruction.

Mercy rejoiceth against judgment: just judgment is to give everyone who has a right his right, but mercy in Christianity gives more than the right that people deserve, as long as they are in need. Whoever does not show mercy to others, so that he shows partiality to the rich and despises the poor, God will not have mercy on him and will sentence him to eternal destruction; rather, the rule of Christianity is mercy, especially since God showed us His mercy in redemption and in forgiving our sins every day, which moves us to have compassion on all and to show them mercy.

God allowed some to suffer poverty or sickness or any need, so that the love and mercy of others toward them might appear, and all might hold together as members of one body and rejoice in the love that binds them and forget their pains; so do not neglect any needy person around you.
The Apostle James found the poor dying of hunger and the rich not moving, so he spoke of the uselessness of faith without works.

This does not contradict the Apostle Paul, who says, “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28), because Paul is speaking of the works of the Law that are not necessary for salvation, and for that reason he spoke of the necessity of faith that works by love and spoke of striving, service and giving. This agrees with the Apostle James, who here speaks of the works that are the fruit of living faith.
In the following verses the Apostle offers practical examples of the necessity of joining good works to faith as a condition for the believer’s salvation.
The first example: the Apostle gives an example. If you have a brother or sister who is poor and you show kindness to them in words without offering a positive deed, you are not meeting their needs.

The second example: faith without works is like a dead body that has no spirit; the spirit is the works, which show that faith is alive. Faith that has no works is theoretical faith, dead in itself, and it leads you to death.

The third example shows the importance of good works in a dialogue that takes place between a person who has faith without works and a second who has good works resulting from his faith. The second says to the first: if your faith is real, show it to me, because it cannot be shown without works, but I by my good works show you that my faith is real.

The fourth example also confirms the uselessness of faith without works. If a person has faith in the one God but has no good works, this profits him nothing but condemns him on the last day, because his faith did not bear good works. It is like the demons, who believe that God is one and recognize this so greatly that they reach the point of great fear of God, which is expressed by trembling, yet they continue in their evils, so this theoretical faith of theirs, not accompanied by good works, condemns them on the last day.

In the true believer the works of love appear in his life, but the “vain man”, that is, the one who has faith without good works, his faith is vain. And the Apostle goes on to prove to him by other evidences that his faith, void of works, is dead.
The fifth example:

The Apostle James uses an example, Abraham, the father of the Jewish people, whose working faith appeared when he offered Isaac his son as a sacrifice, believing that God was able to raise him from the dead (Rom 4:3). Thus the work shared with Abraham’s faith, and by his work his faith was made perfect, that is, by his offering Isaac as a sacrifice he perfected his faith in God, who is able to raise from the dead.
The Friend: a friend.

By works, that is, by Abraham’s offering Isaac his son as a sacrifice, the saying of the Holy Bible in (Gen 15:6) was fulfilled, so he perfected his faith, by which he became righteous before God, and even rose to the degree of friendship with God. And this is the fifth proof that justification takes place by faith and works and not by faith alone.
The sixth example:

The Apostle gives an example of the joining of works to faith among the Gentiles who believed, and not only the Jews. Rahab, the Gentile harlot, believed in the power of the God of Israel and hid the two men whom Joshua had sent to spy out the Promised Land, so that they would not be killed (Josh 2:1-6), and she hung a scarlet cord on her house, a sign of faith in the blood of Christ the Redeemer, so God rescued her from destruction with the idolaters, the inhabitants of Jericho, for her faith that worked by love. By this Rahab declared that works are like the spirit in the body and give it life; if there are no works, faith, which is like the body, will become dead.

Do not be content with appreciating the troubles and needs of others, but join your feelings with works of love that you offer them, even small works, as much as you can, knowing that your work, however small, has value before God, for the cup of cold water will not lose its reward.
The tongue and wisdom

The Apostle James was bishop of Jerusalem and one of the pillars of the Church, and yet he says in humility, “Be not many masters, my brethren,” because he found that some were competing to take on the image of the teacher and guide, and so put themselves in danger, for the following reasons:
(1) Because it gives him a false sense that he is better than others.

(2) Because teaching is in essence a gift of the Holy Spirit, so no one should seize it by his pride. (3) Every teacher receives a greater condemnation, because what he teaches he must first do himself.

(4) “Unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required” (Lk 12:48). (5) Every teacher is exposed to falling, and when Satan makes him fall he scatters the flock. Therefore we find that Arius, who was a skilled orator and went astray, caused many to fall after him.

Every person is exposed to falling into sin, and no one can completely control his tongue except the Perfect One, who is Christ. Whoever controls his tongue can control all his lusts, thoughts and senses. And since a person strives and controls himself to some extent by the grace of God, he should be careful not to rush into teaching others.

Let us therefore take heed in everything we learn and also in what we do. For this reason every person must have a wise father of confession to be a guide for him so that his spiritual life may be set straight, and instead of teaching others, he should first be concerned with the salvation of his own soul, because the war against those who serve is fierce.
The Apostle likens the tongue to three things:

1- The first comparison: he likens the tongue to the bit that is put in the mouths of horses so that the rider may steer them in the direction he wants, because if horses had no bit they would throw and destroy their rider. In the same way, whoever controls his tongue can move his whole body, that is, his conduct, in the way of truth, so that the body does not break loose in its lusts like a horse without a bit.
Let us train ourselves to control the tongue so that by the grace of Christ we may be able to control the lusts of the body.

The second comparison: he likens the tongue to the rudder of a ship, which, though small, lets the helmsman steer a huge ship in the direction he wants, however strong the winds. In the same way the tongue is a small member that we must handle with care in every word we utter, “for by your words you shall be justified, and by your words you shall be condemned” (Mt 12:37). The tongue can defile the whole body and bring judgment on us, though on the other hand it is able to lead a person in peace like the rudder of a ship.
The third comparison: he likens the tongue to a spark, that is, a small fire that can kindle huge fires.
Just as a small spark kindles huge fires, so with one word from the tongue fire is kindled in the world of sin and iniquity, and divisions, hatred and enmity arise among people.

And it setteth on fire: that is, it kindles wars among peoples. The tongue boasts, exalting itself, that it directs the whole universe, and it leads a person to pride and so defiles the whole body, because it brings many evils and then casts the whole body into hell.

Hell (Gehenna): named after the valley of “Hinnom”, which lies southeast of the Temple, below Jerusalem. The blood of sacrifices flowed into it, and the Jews threw into it dead animals and refuse to burn them, so the fires in it were not quenched night and day; hence it is used to refer to the eternal fire.

The fourth comparison: he likens it to poison, because it is easy for a person to tame wild beasts, birds or reptiles, but the insolent tongue that is accustomed to foul speech is hard to tame, though God can of course do so. Sometimes the tongue utters a word, and it comes out like the deadly venom of a serpent and destroys a relationship that took many years to build. Therefore David says in the Psalm, “Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips” (Ps 141:3).

If your tongue affects the salvation of your soul and your relationships with those around you to this degree, may you not rush into speaking, so that you give yourself an opportunity to seek God and to listen attentively to those around you, and God will guide you to the fitting words.

The Apostle rebukes those who curse others: how can they bless God with their tongue in prayers and then trouble people created in the image of God with their bad words? What are they doing: are they blessing God or cursing Him?!
And he declares that this is a grave error that should never be.

The fifth comparison: he likens the tongue to a spring of water, and asks whether it is possible for the same spring to send forth two kinds of water, one sweet and the other bitter?! This is a rhetorical question, meaning that this cannot happen, and therefore it is not right for prayers and bad words to come out of the same tongue. Thus the Apostle James calls us to repent of bad speech.

The sixth comparison: he likens it to a tree, and asks a second rhetorical question: can a tree bear fruit contrary to its kind?! Can a fig tree, for example, bear olives, or a vine figs?! Of course not. So the tongue of the children of God must speak only words of blessing, whether to God in prayers or to people in kind speech.

Because you are a child of God, this must show in your speech with others, in kind words, whether in encouragement, or in apologizing for your mistakes and showing your readiness to help them and cooperate with them, so that you offer the love of God that is in you through your good words.
He speaks to the believers who want to teach others and says to them: whoever among you has wisdom, knowledge and learning, so as to teach another, must show his wisdom in two ways:
1- Sound conduct in the various situations of life, for how can you teach others wisdom while you act in an unsound way?
2- That his sound conduct be accompanied by meekness, that is, calm of heart, and likewise by not being disturbed in his dealings with others.
Glory not, and lie not against the truth: do not think of yourselves that you are wise teachers when you are fallen into sin, and you have human knowledge and wisdom far from God and the truth.

The Apostle draws a comparison between earthly wisdom and heavenly wisdom. Earthly wisdom springs from love of the world, so that brother tramples on brother for the sake of money, and it is “sensual”, that is, it comes from the human self (the ego), like teachings that take a religious form and have an emotional effect and suggest holiness and piety to the soul, but are far from spiritual things. The true saint, however, always feels that he is a sinner and in need of repentance the nearer he comes to the divine throne, like the prophet Isaiah. The spiritual life usually has no violent leaps, but grows gradually like a plant, or like a child: when you give him a meal he does not grow up suddenly, but grows day by day.

Earthly wisdom is also “devilish”, that is, its hidden motive is Satan, who suggests to a person that he alone is wise, and so brings into him the spirit of pride and envy, and divisions, confusion, deviations, factions and partiality arise, and heresies come into being under the cover of this wisdom.
Heavenly wisdom is given by God to whoever asks in faith, not wavering, and its characteristics are:
1- Pure: that is, clean, with no crooked purpose, far from partiality; its possessor practices a pure religion that shows in visiting widows and orphans.

2- Peaceable: because its source is the King of peace, and not as the world gives a temporary peace; it is peacemaking, so peace and calm spread between a person and himself, between him and God, and between him and people.

3- Gentle: toward the mistakes of others, it embraces them, bears their weakness and encourages them to repent, like the gentleness of Christ and His encouragement of Zacchaeus the chief of the tax collectors (Lk 19:1-10) and of the sinful woman in the house of Simon the Pharisee (Lk 7:36-50).

4- Easy to be entreated: this means readiness to obey the divine commandment, the Church and parents, as it is said of Christ that He was subject to His mother the Virgin and Joseph the carpenter (Lk 2:51); it also listens to others, but with discernment, without being led or yielding to mistaken opinions.

5- Full of mercy and good fruits: heavenly wisdom bears fruits of mercy and good works toward the weak, sinners, the needy, the poor, the sick and the fainthearted, resting on living faith that works by love.
6- Without partiality: that is, firm in the love of God and faith in Him, far from doubt and wavering.
7- Without hypocrisy: that is, what is inside the heart is what appears on a person in his conduct and behavior.
8- The fruit of righteousness: heavenly wisdom sows peace, so it bears righteousness and good, pure works.

May we humble ourselves before God and others and ask Him for wisdom, and He will teach us how to act and speak with those around us, keeping purity and repentance, so that He may continue to work in us by His Holy Spirit and give us His wisdom. Evil desires
Your lusts that war in your members: the evil desires that draw the members of the body to the pleasure of sin.
Evil desires cause serious results in a person’s life, the most important of which are:

(1) Problems between people: the desires of sin make people differ with one another and clash, because they produce selfishness in the heart and so cause quarrels and problems, even violent wars, between people.
Because ye ask not: you do not seek God and the spiritual life with Him.

(2) Never being satisfied: the evil desires that produce selfishness in a person make him greedy, so he runs after desires and uses every means of evil, such as sins of the flesh, quarreling and murder, but he is not satisfied with his desire; rather his thirst for it increases, like one who runs after a mirage and is never quenched but is lost in the wilderness of the world, because he does not seek God and spiritual things but only his material desires, which increase his thirst.

(3) Corruption of the relationship with God: the Apostle shows that indulgence in desires corrupts the relationship with God, for their prayers turn toward material requests and leave the love of God and of others, and therefore God does not answer them, and they receive nothing of what they asked, because they ask for their evil desires.
(4) The enmity of God:

The Holy Bible likens God’s relationship with His people to the bond of a bridegroom with his bride and counts the believer’s love of the world as spiritual adultery, so it declares plainly that it is enmity with God, because it takes a person away from Him, and he is occupied with love of the world, which should have been only a bridge to cross over to the heavenly wedding. God asks us for love with all our hearts, as a husband who expects from his bride her whole heart. Therefore the Apostle Paul says, “For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor 11:2); that is, every person has freedom of will to choose either to love God and hate the world, or to love the world and hate God.
The spirit that dwelleth in us: the Holy Spirit who dwelt in us in the sacrament of the Holy Myron.

Lusteth to envy: He loves us and is jealous over us because of the devil’s dominion, and strives to return us to His love. Whoever loves the world and clings to material things is an enemy of God. The whole Holy Bible declares God’s love for us and His jealousy over us, and the Holy Spirit who dwelt in us in the sacrament of the Holy Myron is jealous over us if we cling to desires and material things. He does not stand against us if we are hostile to Him, but in His love He wants to bring us back to Him and deliver us from the grip of the devil, and even gives us grace to resist the wars of Satan, and then gives us the enjoyment of peace, joy and delight in His fellowship.

5- Pride: desires produce pride, which makes a person increase in desires, lose the grace of God and resist Him, so that He is angry with him for his stubbornness. On the other hand, whoever humbles himself before God, He delivers him from his sins and gives him the enjoyment of His fellowship.

If you are fought by any desire, humble yourself before God in repentance and humility so that He may remove it from you, and do not be troubled however much you fall, but persevere in your striving and be careful to keep away from the sources of these desires.

Humility and submission to God by obeying His commandments support a person with strength to resist the wars of the devil so that he does not fear him, but on the contrary the devil fears the power of God and keeps away from this striving person.

Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you: draw near to God by prayer, by reading His holy word and by partaking of the Holy Mysteries; then you will feel His nearness to you, for He is near to you, and your drawing near to Him is a response to His love, and then you will feel that He draws near to you, and you will enjoy His care and providence more than before.
Cleanse your hands, ye sinners: by repenting of your sins, which show in your conduct and works, indicated by the hands.

Purify your hearts, ye double minded: you who waver between love of the world and love of God, be purified from this wavering and reject love of the world, so that you may be of one mind, which is love of God.
He calls them to prayer, to reading the Holy Bible and to repentance of sins, so that they may walk in the love of God.
He calls them to deep repentance with contrition and tears, in distress over sin, instead of indulging in the joys of desires, their corrupt pleasures and their wicked laughter.

If they feel the horror of their sins they will repent in humility, asking for God’s help and forgiveness, and to the extent that they humble themselves before Him, He removes their sins from them and blesses them, and even glorifies them and gives them the enjoyment of His love.

The Apostle forbids them to judge, because it is not only against the one they judge but also against the Law, which commands love of neighbor. Whoever judges breaks the Law and becomes opposed to it, that is, it condemns him because of his deeds, which are the judging of another.

God is the giver of the Law, and He alone is the Judge of the whole world. How then do you dare, O man, to judge another? By this you usurp the place of God the Judge and expose yourself to His judgment and punishment, for God in His mercy is able to lead your brothers who have fallen into sin so that they are saved, while you perish because of your insistence on judging.

Be concerned with your own repentance, and make excuses for those who sin around you, and to the extent of your humility before God His mercies will overflow upon you. Be positive and concerned with your repentance and your striving against sin, and as for others who fall into sin like you, pray for them, that God may have mercy on you and on them.

He rebukes those who rely on their own strength and are occupied with love of money, who go from place to place for trade and profit without relying on God. Trade is not wrong in itself, but not relying on God is the wrong.

He warns them that they do not know when their life will end, because the life of man is short, and he likens it to vapor, which appears large in shape but quickly vanishes. Therefore one should seize the opportunity of life to repent of the love of money and of all sins and to care for the salvation of the soul; and as for the works of the world, one should rely on God in them, and God should remain the only goal of life.
The Apostle here makes clear the sound conduct, which is to rely on God and then to practice any work or trade. Prayer is essential before beginning any work.
He also rebukes their pride and their boasting in their strength and their money, for this pride is evil and rejected by God, and even brings His wrath upon men.

Lest some become lazy about working, he warns us of the importance of doing all good duties, for everything good and useful must be committed to, whether in material or spiritual works, relying on God in them, and every opportunity to do good should be seized, because life is short and will quickly end, and since God has given us the opportunity to work, how can we neglect it?! Work is a blessing because it is for God’s sake and not a heavy duty, and wasting opportunities for work is counted a sin for which a person is held to account before God.

Be concerned not only to keep away from evil but also to do good and seize every opportunity to encourage and support those around you; and if you were negligent, offer repentance for that before your father of confession, and then rise to seize new opportunities to do good.
Asceticism, patience, prayer and service

entries.section: (1) The end of the love of money

paragraphs.text: Your miseries that shall come upon you: eternal torment.
Are corrupted: dissipated.
Motheaten: the moth is a small insect that eats clothes.

The Apostle James calls the rich who rely on their money to weep and howl, because their miseries are coming. They were occupied with gathering earthly treasures and loved perishable things more than God. He describes what will happen to them: their riches will be dissipated and their garments will be corrupted and eaten by moths. Even the precious metals will rust and lose their shine, and all this will be a witness against them and a cause of their torment in the fire of hell, because the poor man was in need and they did not give to him, and even in the last days of their life, instead of being occupied with the heavenly treasure, they were occupied with gathering perishable earthly treasures, so they lost everything on earth and in heaven, and in the end themselves.

entries.section: (1) The end of the love of money

paragraphs.text: Kept back by fraud: you reduced the wages of those who work in them, that is, you gave them less than their due.

The love of money leads to selfishness and cruelty, and here is the wage of the laborer who sowed and reaped the fields of the rich, which they have unjustly withheld from him; and the cry of those wronged people has been heard by the mighty God, expressed as “the Lord of sabaoth”, who is able to do all things and defends the wronged.

entries.section: (1) The end of the love of money

paragraphs.text: The rich live in luxury and ease, as if they were fattening their hearts, which have become hardened by sin, like fatted calves for the day of slaughter, so that the fattened body becomes food for worms, as the Holy Bible says, “But she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth” (1 Tim 5:6).

entries.section: (1) The end of the love of money

paragraphs.text: They have also condemned the innocent and weak and imprisoned him, and the poor man they have killed with hunger, and he cannot resist them.

The Apostle James gives us his practical teachings, that the treasures of the world perish and vanish, so lay up for yourself treasure in heaven, as the Lord Christ said in (Mt 6:19). So if you meet a poor man, or an opportunity to do good, do it, and trust that it is a precious opportunity God has given you, so do not waste it, for it will not return again.
The precious fruit of the earth: the fruits of the harvest, which signify the eternal reward.

The early rain: which waters the winter crops in the autumn season, and signifies the work of the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of Baptism and His encouragement of believers at the beginning of their spiritual striving.

The latter rain: which waters the winter crops at the beginning of spring, a short time before the harvest ripens, and signifies the help of the Holy Spirit to believers during their striving and until the end of their life.

He calls the poor and the wronged to stand firm in the faith, to be patient and to take a lesson from the farmer, who sows and plows and waits patiently for the crop until it drinks the early rain of autumn and the latter rain of spring, and to wait for the salvation of the Lord and His coming, when He will reward them in eternity, for whoever looks to Christ in His coming finds his sufferings easy.
Grudge not: do not murmur.

He commands that the poor and wronged man not murmur against the rich man nor judge him or seek vengeance on him, because the rich man is wretched and held in the hand of Satan, and lest the poor man be condemned for his murmuring. And let him remember that Christ will come as Judge to give each one according to his works (Mt 7:1).

The Apostle calls them to be patient and to wait for the salvation of the Lord, because He does not let them be tempted above what they are able to bear, and he put before them the prophets’ patient endurance of suffering so that they may follow their example.

He gave them an example of patience, which is “Job”, and how God rewarded him, because he endured the death of his children, sickness, poverty and mockery, so God praised him and then gave him twice as much as he had had.

The Gospel forbids swearing, for how can we swear by something we do not own?! Everything we own belongs to God and we are stewards over it. If your speech is always truthful, people will trust you, because the upright tongue speaks one word, without interpretation or twisting. The true Christian, who is always truthful in his speech, does not need to swear for people to believe him, as the Lord Christ said, “Swear not at all” (Mt 5:34). On the other hand, it is not fitting for us to swear by the name of God or by anything else, because Satan exploits the word of an oath in an hour of anger, as happened when Herod killed John the Baptist (Mt 14:7).

entries.section: (3) Prayer and the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick

paragraphs.text: He calls them, if they meet with afflictions and trials, to lift up their hearts to God, who feels for them and suffered for them on the Cross, so He supports them and they do not feel weary because of their great sense of God’s consolations. And if God gives them gifts and delivers them from trials, let them express their joy in a spiritual way and not in evil like the people of the world. The expression of joy is by praise and psalm-singing, and therefore the Church has arranged hymns of praise that are said every day, in addition to the hymns of the various occasions.

entries.section: (3) Prayer and the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick

paragraphs.text: Elders: priests, which is the correct translation in the Greek language and also in the versions approved by the Orthodox and Catholic Churches, but in the Protestant versions we have at hand the word was translated “elders” because the Protestants do not believe in the sacrament of the priesthood.

The Apostle James affirms that the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick was established and practiced in the apostolic age, and he directs the believers’ attention to calling the priests, that is, the clergy, to visit the house where there is a sick person, to pray over him the prayer of the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick and to anoint him with the oil upon which the Holy Spirit has descended through prayer.

entries.section: (3) Prayer and the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick

paragraphs.text: He stresses the importance of faith in the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick so that the sick person may be healed, whether his own faith or the faith of the priests or the faith of those around him, and he adds to this the necessity of repentance and confession of sin before the priests present during this sacrament, so that the sick receive forgiveness of their sins in addition to healing from their bodily illnesses.

entries.section: (3) Prayer and the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick

paragraphs.text: The sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick was practiced with a large number of people present in the house. Seven priests would come, or at least more than one priest in the case of severe illnesses, and in this gathering he calls those present to confess their sins before the priests present, so that the first group is the people and the second group is the priests. Of course it is unreasonable that he means the priests confessing before the people, or the people confessing to one another leaving aside the priests who are present.

He also asks those present to pray with one heart for the sick person so that he may be healed, and that this should be their constant conduct, praying for one another; and here he singles out especially the priests who lead the prayer during this sacrament.

He stresses the value of prayer that comes from a pure heart before God, for it is able to heal diseases. Here appears the importance of intercession, which the early Church held to in the days of the Apostles. The “righteous man” is of course the saint, and the intercession of the saints is able to do many things and God rejoices in it, because whoever holds to it shows his humility and faith, and likewise his love for the saints.

entries.section: (3) Prayer and the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick

paragraphs.text: The Apostle confirms his words with the story of the prophet Elijah (1 Kgs 17:1), who was a man of human nature like us, exposed to sufferings and afflictions, and prayed in faith that it might not rain, and the rain stopped for three years and a half, in order to call the people to repentance and the worship of God and to leave the worship of idols; and when many of them returned to God, he prayed a second time and the rain fell, and the earth sprouted and bore fruit and the famine ended. Thus appear the importance of the prayers of the saints and God’s concern to answer them.

Prayer is a power that moves the whole world and draws down the mercies of God, especially if it comes from a repentant, pure heart in need of God, in supplication and faith. So do not delay, but hasten to God in all your needs and press Him however great your request, trusting in His love and mercy.

entries.section: (4) Visiting those who have gone astray

paragraphs.text: He urges the believers to care for one another, so that if one of them departs from the faith or goes astray into grave sins, they should hasten to care for him and call him to repentance with humility and love, and so save him from eternal destruction, so that his sins are not exposed before the Church, but he returns a living member in her.

Here appears the importance of service. God is the Savior, but He rejoices in our spiritual service to one another and blesses it and completes it. St. Gregory affirmed this meaning with his words, “If the one who saves a person from bodily death, though he will die some day, deserves a reward, how much more does he deserve who saves a soul from eternal death.”

These verses confirm the possibility of a believer’s perishing and answer the Protestant innovations that say the opposite, and the Apostle Paul confirms the same meaning with his words, “Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him” (Heb 10:38), and he also says, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil 2:12). Then he proves it with real evidence when he says, “For many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you even weeping, that they are the enemies of the cross of Christ” (Phil 3:18).
Care for the salvation of those around you, especially your household, relatives and friends, and if they do not accept your direct word, offer them love and care and pray for them.
